question: Who is known as the 'Father of History'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Herodotus.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Herodotus, a Greek writer, is called the Father of History; his book is titled 'Histories', an account of the Greco-Persian wars along with the customs of many peoples (इतिहास का पिता — हेरोडोटस)

 

• The title was conferred on him by the Roman orator Cicero, not by Herodotus himself.

 

• He is called the Father of History because he was among the first to collect and arrange past events systematically as a narrative.

 

• In SSC exams, the Herodotus/Cicero link and the book name 'Histories' are asked repeatedly.

 

• Herodotus wrote about the Greco-Persian wars and the lands and customs of the peoples involved, and his habit of collecting and sifting accounts is why later writers saw him as the first to treat the past as a subject of inquiry.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Cicero lived in the first century BC and is remembered as a Roman orator, lawyer and politician; the Father of History title came from his writing about Herodotus.

 

• Herodotus's work deals with the Greco-Persian wars, which makes the Histories one of the earliest large prose narratives of the ancient world.

 

• Do not confuse Herodotus with Thucydides, who wrote on the Peloponnesian War, or with Kalhana, whose Rajatarangini is the Kashmir chronicle.

 

• Megasthenes's Indica is the Greek account of Mauryan India, so Greek authors matter in Indian history questions as well.

 

NOTE

 

• Cicero (Option 2): Cicero was a Roman statesman and orator of the first century BC who gave Herodotus the title, so he is the one who honoured the Father of History rather than the Father himself. Cicero was a Roman statesman and orator who gave the title to Herodotus; he is not himself the Father of History.

 

• Megasthenes (Option 3): Megasthenes was the Greek ambassador of Seleucus Nicator at Chandragupta Maurya's court and wrote the Indica, which survives only in quotations by later writers. Megasthenes was a Seleucid ambassador in the Mauryan court who wrote 'Indica', not the Father of History.

 

• Kalhana (Option 4): Kalhana was a twelfth-century Kashmiri poet-historian who wrote the Rajatarangini, the chronicle of the kings of Kashmir, and is often called India's earliest true historian. Kalhana was a Kashmiri chronicler who wrote 'Rajatarangini', a history of Kashmir.

question:
Consider the following statements:

1. Herodotus was a Greek historian.

2. His book is called 'Histories'.

3. The title 'Father of History' was given to him by Cicero.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• All three statements are correct: Herodotus was a Greek historian, his work is 'Histories' and the Roman orator Cicero gave him the title Father of History (तीनों कथन सही — हेरोडोटस, हिस्टोरीज़, सिसेरो)

 

• Statement 1 is correct because Herodotus belonged to Greece (born at Halicarnassus).

 

• Statement 2 is correct because his famous work is named Histories.

 

• Statement 3 is correct because it was Cicero who first called him Father of History.

 

• The three statements form a standard exam trio: nationality (Greek), book (Histories) and the title-giver (Cicero). Questions often reverse the last two, so remember that Cicero is the Roman who praised him, not the author.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Halicarnassus, the birthplace of Herodotus, lay in Asia Minor and belonged to the Greek world of the fifth century BC.

 

• The word history comes from the Greek historia, which means inquiry, matching the way Herodotus gathered information by asking questions.

 

• Cicero is also known for his speeches and letters, and he was Roman, not Greek, which is a common trap in match questions.

 

• SSC often asks three-part factual questions on Herodotus: nationality, book name and the person who gave him the title.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 2 only (Option 1): It is correct about statements 1 and 2 but wrongly leaves out statement 3, which is true because the title Father of History was indeed conferred by Cicero. This leaves out statement 3, which is also correct since Cicero gave him the title.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): It is correct about statements 2 and 3 but wrongly leaves out statement 1, although Herodotus was undoubtedly a Greek historian from Halicarnassus. This leaves out statement 1, which is also correct since Herodotus was Greek.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 4): It is correct about statements 1 and 3 but wrongly leaves out statement 2, although Herodotus's book is certainly named Histories. This leaves out statement 2, which is also correct since his book is 'Histories'.

question: The abbreviation 'A.D.' stands for:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Anno Domini.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A.D. stands for Anno Domini, a Latin phrase meaning 'in the year of the Lord'; it counts years after the birth of Christ (ए.डी. — ईसवी सन्)

 

• B.C. stands for Before Christ and covers years before the birth of Christ.

 

• In the notes' scheme, history runs from about 1000 BC to AD times, when records were both written and readable.

 

• A.D. is a Latin phrase, not an English one, which is why 'After Death' is a common wrong guess.

 

• The two era labels are mirror images: B.C. counts backwards towards the birth of Christ, while A.D. counts forwards from it. A.D. is placed before the year (AD 2025) whereas B.C. is placed after it (1000 BC).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Years in the Common Era system are written as CE and BCE, which are modern neutral equivalents of AD and BC.

 

• There is no year zero in this count; 1 BC is followed directly by AD 1.

 

• The Christian era was fixed in the sixth century AD by the monk Dionysius Exiguus, a fact that appears occasionally in general knowledge papers.

 

• The notes place History proper from about 1000 BC to the present, so both BC and AD dates fall within the historic age.

 

NOTE

 

• Ante Diem (Option 2): Ante Diem is a Latin phrase meaning 'before the day' and appears in Roman date reckoning, but it has nothing to do with the Christian era abbreviation. 'Ante Diem' means 'before the day' in Latin and is not the expansion of A.D.

 

• Annual Date (Option 3): Annual Date is not a Latin or standard expansion at all; it is a made-up phrase that merely sounds similar to the initials A.D. 'Annual Date' is not a valid expansion; A.D. is Latin.

 

• After Death (Option 4): After Death is the popular but mistaken reading of A.D.; the abbreviation counts years from the birth of Christ, not from his death, and its Latin form is Anno Domini. 'After Death' is a popular misreading; A.D. refers to the year of the Lord, not the death of Christ.

question: The period in which people knew the art of writing but their script has not been deciphered is called:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Protohistory.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• This is Protohistory (c. 3000 BC–1000 BC): people knew writing, but it is not readable today; the Indus Valley Civilisation is the standard example (आद्य इतिहास — सिंधु सभ्यता, अपठित लिपि)

 

• Indian history is divided into three parts depending on whether writing existed and whether it can be read now.

 

• The undeciphered Indus script is the reason the Harappan period is classed as protohistoric.

 

• Only when records are both written and readable do we enter 'History' proper.

 

• The Indus Valley Civilisation is the textbook protohistoric culture: its people certainly had writing on seals, but because the script has never been deciphered, historians cannot treat it as a readable written record and so keep it out of History proper.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Protohistory in the notes covers about 3000 BC to 1000 BC and lies between the nonliterate Stone Age and the readable historic age.

 

• Mesopotamian and Egyptian scripts were deciphered, but the Indus script remains an unsolved puzzle despite hundreds of seals with short inscriptions.

 

• The Vedic literature belongs to the period around the end of Protohistory, as it was composed and preserved orally.

 

• The term protohistory is a favourite in comprehension-type questions on the three divisions of Indian history.

 

NOTE

 

• Pre-history (Option 1): Pre-history is the stage before writing was known, which in India means the Stone Age, and it is reconstructed only from stone tools, bones, pots and paintings. Pre-history is the stage with no writing at all, known only through stone, bones and pots.

 

• History (Option 2): History in the strict sense begins when records are both written and readable, dated in the notes from about 1000 BC, which excludes the undeciphered Indus script. History requires records that are both written and readable, which the Harappan seals are not.

 

• Chalcolithic Age (Option 3): Chalcolithic Age is a cultural phase marked by the use of copper along with stone, not a division based on writing; Harappan and other cultures can fall under it. Chalcolithic Age is a cultural/technological phase (copper plus stone), not a division based on writing.

question:
Match the terms in Column A with Column B:

Column A: (a) Herodotus  (b) Cicero  (c) Protohistory  (d) Pre-history

Column B: (i) Gave the title 'Father of History'  (ii) Greek author of 'Histories'  (iii) Writing existed but unreadable  (iv) No writing, Stone Age
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct matching is a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv: Herodotus wrote Histories; Cicero gave him the title; Protohistory has unreadable writing (Indus); Pre-history has no writing (Stone Age) (सही मिलान — हेरोडोटस, सिसेरो, आद्य इतिहास, प्रागैतिहास)

 

• Pre-history is dated in the notes from the earliest times to about 3000 BC and is known only from stone, sand and pots.

 

• Protohistory covers roughly 3000 BC to 1000 BC.

 

• Herodotus and Cicero are a classic SSC pair.

 

• Match questions of this kind reward learning the two sets of definitions together: the person who wrote (Herodotus), the person who named him (Cicero), and the two eras defined by the state of writing (Protohistory and Pre-history).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Roman writers like Cicero are not authors of Indian history, but their comments on Greek historians appear in SSC questions about the origin of history.

 

• Stone Age, Pre-history and Palaeolithic-to-Neolithic are linked terms; a good review method is to place each on a timeline.

 

• Protohistory has one famous example in India, the Indus Valley Civilisation, so any match with unreadable writing should point to it.

 

• Herodotus is Greek, Cicero is Roman, Kalhana is Indian, and this three-way contrast is a typical exam trap.

 

NOTE

 

• a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv (Option 1): This pairs Herodotus with the title-giving role and Cicero with the book, which reverses them: Herodotus authored Histories and Cicero gave him the title. This swaps Herodotus and Cicero; Herodotus wrote the book while Cicero gave the title.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii (Option 3): This correctly pairs the two writers but wrongly links Protohistory with no writing and Pre-history with unreadable script, which is the reverse of the true definitions. This swaps Protohistory and Pre-history; Protohistory has unreadable writing, Pre-history has none.

 

• a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i (Option 4): This is a scrambled matching that ties Herodotus to unreadable writing and Cicero to the Stone Age, neither of which has any basis. This is a completely scrambled matching, linking Herodotus with unreadable writing.

question:
Assertion (A): No literary works exist from the Pre-historic period.

Reason (R): Writing was unknown to the people of the Stone Age.

Select the correct option:
option_1: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true, but R is false
option_4: A is false, but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both are true and R explains A: since writing was unknown in the Stone Age, no literary works exist, and knowledge comes from archaeological evidence such as stone, bones and pots (प्रागैतिहास — लेखन का अभाव)

 

• Pre-history is therefore reconstructed from tools, paintings, bones and settlement remains.

 

• This is why pre-historic period is defined mainly by the absence of writing.

 

• Archaeology, not literature, is the chief source for this period.

 

• The logic runs in a chain: no writing, therefore no literature, therefore the only evidence is material. This explains why archaeology, rather than texts, is the main tool for the pre-historic period.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Because the Stone Age has no texts, archaeologists date material by layers of earth and later by scientific methods such as radiocarbon dating.

 

• Stone tools, bones, pots and sand layers are the evidence named in the notes for the pre-historic period.

 

• Literature begins to matter only from the historic period, when texts like the Vedas, epics and inscriptions are available.

 

• Questions on assertion and reason often use the logic of absence of evidence, so train yourself to link cause and effect.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 2): R is not merely a related remark; the absence of writing is the direct reason that no literary works from the Stone Age exist, so it does explain A. R is not just true but also the direct cause of A, so a mere 'not explanation' verdict is wrong.

 

• A is true, but R is false (Option 3): A is true because no literary works exist from the pre-historic period, and R is also true because writing was unknown, so the second part fails. R is true: writing really was unknown in the Stone Age, so 'R is false' is wrong.

 

• A is false, but R is true (Option 4): A is true because pre-history is known only through archaeological evidence, so calling the assertion false is wrong even though R is correct. A is true: no literary works exist from this period, so 'A is false' is wrong.

question: What is the main characteristic of the Prehistoric period in India?
option_3: Stone tools and absence of writing
solution_text:
The correct answer is Stone tools and absence of writing.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Prehistoric period is characterised by stone tools and the absence of writing; knowledge comes from archaeological finds like tools, bones and pots (प्रागैतिहास — पाषाण उपकरण, लेखन नहीं)

 

• The Stone Age is the Indian pre-history; people did not know writing, so there are no literary works.

 

• Stone tools help historians understand early human lifestyle and survival techniques.

 

• Metals appear only in the later Chalcolithic (copper) phase.

 

• Notice the pairing in the correct answer: stone tools are what survive, and absence of writing is what defines the period. Together they separate pre-history from both protohistory (unreadable writing) and history (readable writing).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rock paintings such as those at Bhimbetka are among the most direct records left by pre-historic humans.

 

• The Stone Age is the whole of Indian Pre-history, whereas the Metal Age brings in copper and leads into protohistoric cultures.

 

• Written records, coins and inscriptions are the tools of the historian of later ages, not of the pre-historian.

 

• Stone tool studies also reveal which animals were hunted and how food was processed.

 

NOTE

 

• Written records (Option 1): Written records belong to the historic period; their absence is precisely what defines pre-history, so this choice states the opposite of the truth. Written records are absent in pre-history; they belong to the historic period.

 

• Metal tools (Option 2): Metal tools came with the Chalcolithic phase, when copper was first used; the earlier Stone Age phases used only tools of stone. Metal tools began with copper in the Chalcolithic phase, after the pure stone phases.

 

• Coins display (Option 4): Coins appear in the historic period, with punch-marked coins belonging to the age of the Mahajanapadas, long after the Stone Age. Coins belong to the historic period and are unrelated to the Stone Age.

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four phases into which Indian prehistory is broken in the notes?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vedic Age.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The four phases are Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic and the Metal Age (Chalcolithic); the Vedic Age is a historical/cultural period, not a prehistoric phase (वैदिक काल पाषाण कालीन चरण नहीं)

 

• Palaeolithic = Old Stone Age; Mesolithic = Middle Stone Age; Neolithic = New Stone Age.

 

• The fourth phase is the Metal Age, beginning with copper (Chalcolithic).

 

• The Vedic Age belongs to the later protohistoric/early historic phase.

 

• The Vedic Age is placed after the Stone Age phases and is known from the Vedic literature, which is a written source (though transmitted orally for long). That is why it is never listed among prehistoric phases.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Vedic Age is usually divided into Early (Rig Vedic) and Later Vedic periods and comes within the early historic phase, not the Stone Age.

 

• Bronze Age and Iron Age are terms used elsewhere in the world; in India the metal phase begins with the Chalcolithic.

 

• A NOT-type question is solved by first writing the true list and then spotting the outsider.

 

• Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic together are called the Stone Age, with the metal phase added as the fourth step.

 

NOTE

 

• Palaeolithic (Option 1): Palaeolithic, the Old Stone Age before 10000 BC, is indeed the first of the four phases, so it cannot be the exception asked for in a NOT question. Palaeolithic is the first phase of Indian prehistory.

 

• Mesolithic (Option 2): Mesolithic, the Middle Stone Age dated about 10000 to 6000 BC, is the second listed phase and therefore is part of the scheme, not the exception. Mesolithic is the second phase of Indian prehistory.

 

• Neolithic (Option 3): Neolithic, the New Stone Age marked by agriculture and polished tools, is the third listed phase, so it belongs to the scheme as well. Neolithic is the third phase of Indian prehistory.

question:
Match the Greek word parts in Column A with their meanings in Column B:

Column A: (a) Palaeo  (b) Meso  (c) Neo  (d) Chalco

Column B: (i) New  (ii) Old  (iii) Copper  (iv) Middle
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Palaeo = old, Meso = middle, Neo = new, Chalco = copper, and lithic = stone, so the correct match is a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii (पुरा = पुराना, मध्य = बीच का, नव = नया, ताम्र = तांबा)

 

• Palaeolithic is thus the Old Stone Age and Mesolithic the Middle Stone Age.

 

• Neolithic is the New Stone Age.

 

• Chalcolithic literally means copper-stone.

 

• The prefixes Palaeo, Meso and Neo always indicate a time order, and the last word of each phase name, lithic, stays the same. Chalco replaces the stone idea with copper, marking the entry of metal into human life.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• In Greek, lithos means stone and palaios means old, which is how the term Palaeolithic was coined.

 

• The chronological order of the stone ages is easy to remember as old, middle, new, followed by copper.

 

• The suffix lithic is common to Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic and Chalcolithic.

 

• Copper's chemical symbol is Cu, a point the notes mention while describing the first metal.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii (Option 1): This reverses the meanings of Palaeo and Meso, giving 'middle' to Palaeo and 'old' to Meso, though Palaeo means old and Meso means middle. This swaps old and middle; Palaeo means old and Meso means middle.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii (Option 3): This gives Neo the meaning 'middle' and Meso the meaning 'new', which is wrong as Neo means new and Meso means middle. This pairs Meso with 'new' and Neo with 'middle', which is reversed.

 

• a-i, b-iv, c-ii, d-iii (Option 4): This gives Palaeo the meaning 'new' and Neo 'old', exactly reversing them; Palaeolithic is the Old Stone Age and Neolithic the New Stone Age. This pairs Palaeo with 'new' and Neo with 'old', which is reversed.

question: Palaeolithic people are called hunter-gatherers because:
option_3: They made pottery for storing grain
option_4: They hunted animals and collected edible plants and tubers
solution_text:
The correct answer is They hunted animals and collected edible plants and tubers.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Palaeolithic people did not farm; their food came from hunting animals and gathering edible plants and tubers, hence the term hunter-gatherers (आखेटक-संग्राहक — पुरापाषाण)

 

• Their tools were stone pieces, hand-sized and flaked off large pebbles, used to hunt animals.

 

• They had no settled life as they moved in search of food.

 

• Agriculture, domestication and pottery are later developments of the Mesolithic/Neolithic ages.

 

• The phrase hunter-gatherer describes the whole economy: hunting provided animal food and gathering provided plants and tubers. A group that depends on such wild food has to keep moving, which leaves little room for permanent villages.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The phrase hunter-gatherer is also applied to modern forest peoples who still depend on wild food, which helps students understand the term.

 

• Palaeolithic remains are found at Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh and Bellary in Karnataka.

 

• Tubers are underground plant parts like roots rich in starch, and they formed part of the gathered diet.

 

• Pottery, farming and domestication are collectively the Neolithic package, which is the contrast to the Palaeolithic economy.

 

NOTE

 

• They cultivated wheat and barley (Option 1): Cultivation of wheat and barley is associated with the Neolithic farmers of sites such as Mehrgarh, so it cannot explain why earlier people were called hunter-gatherers. Cultivation of crops began much later, so Palaeolithic people did not farm.

 

• They domesticated cattle and sheep (Option 2): Domestication of animals began in the Mesolithic age, with the dog as the first pet, and was extended in the Neolithic, long after the Palaeolithic. Animal domestication began in the Mesolithic age, not the Palaeolithic.

 

• They made pottery for storing grain (Option 3): Pottery manufacture is one of the four features of the Neolithic Age; Palaeolithic people had only stone tools and no pots to store grain. Pottery manufacture is a Neolithic feature.

question: Handaxes, cleavers and chopping tools are characteristic of which phase of the Palaeolithic Age?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lower Palaeolithic.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Handaxes, cleavers and chopping tools mark the Lower Palaeolithic phase, the earliest division of the Old Stone Age (निम्न पुरापाषाण — हस्तकुठार, विदारणी)

 

• The Palaeolithic Age is divided into Lower, Middle and Upper phases on the basis of the changing tool types.

 

• These were hand-sized stone tools flaked off large pebbles, used mainly for hunting and cutting.

 

• Later phases saw lighter and more specialised tools.

 

• The handaxe is the signature tool of this earliest phase; cleavers and chopping tools were used for cutting, chopping and butchering animals. Such large core tools were made by chipping a pebble on one or both sides.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Lower Palaeolithic is the oldest phase, followed by the Middle and then the Upper Palaeolithic.

 

• Cleavers are heavy tools with a straight cutting edge, and chopping tools were pebbles flaked on one side to make a chopping edge.

 

• Flake tools, scrapers and points belong to the Middle Palaeolithic, which is the next phase.

 

• Microliths, the Mesolithic tool, are smaller than any Palaeolithic tool.

 

NOTE

 

• Middle Palaeolithic (Option 1): Middle Palaeolithic tools are flake tools, scrapers and points, which are lighter and more specialised than the heavy handaxes of the earliest phase. Middle Palaeolithic is marked by flake tools, scrapers and points.

 

• Upper Palaeolithic (Option 2): Upper Palaeolithic tools are blades, burins and scrapers, representing the most advanced tool-making of the Old Stone Age. Upper Palaeolithic is marked by blades, burins and scrapers.

 

• Mesolithic (Option 4): Mesolithic tools are tiny microliths, usually not longer than five centimetres, which are very different from large handaxes and cleavers. Mesolithic tools are tiny microliths, not handaxes.

question: Blades and burins are the typical tools of which phase?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Upper Palaeolithic.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Blades, burins and scrapers are typical of the Upper Palaeolithic, the last phase of the Old Stone Age, showing finer and more specialised tools (उच्च पुरापाषाण — ब्लेड, तक्षणी)

 

• A burin is a chisel-like tool used for engraving or working bone, antler and wood.

 

• The shift to blade technology reflects technological improvement over earlier flake and handaxe traditions.

 

• Upper Palaeolithic precedes the Mesolithic, which brought microliths.

 

• Blades are long, thin and parallel-sided flakes struck from a prepared core, and the burin is a chisel-like tool for engraving and working bone or wood. Both show a more planned technique than the earlier flake or handaxe tools.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Upper Palaeolithic is the last phase of the Old Stone Age and comes just before the Mesolithic.

 

• Scrapers occur in both the Middle and Upper Palaeolithic according to the notes, so they are not a good clue for telling these two apart.

 

• Burins are used to engrave or cut grooves in bone, antler and wood.

 

• The Mesolithic follows with microliths, which are tiny stone pieces of about five centimetres or less.

 

NOTE

 

• Lower Palaeolithic (Option 1): Lower Palaeolithic tools are handaxes, cleavers and chopping tools, the oldest and heaviest tool types of the Old Stone Age. Lower Palaeolithic tools are handaxes, cleavers and chopping tools.

 

• Middle Palaeolithic (Option 3): Middle Palaeolithic tools are flake tools, scrapers and points, which came between the heavy handaxes and the later blades. Middle Palaeolithic tools are flake tools, scrapers and points.

 

• Neolithic (Option 4): Neolithic tools are polished stone implements linked to farming and settled life, a far later development than blades and burins. Neolithic tools are polished stone tools, associated with agriculture.

question:
Match the Palaeolithic phases in Column A with their tools in Column B:

Column A: (a) Lower Palaeolithic  (b) Middle Palaeolithic  (c) Upper Palaeolithic  (d) Mesolithic

Column B: (i) Blades and burins  (ii) Microliths  (iii) Handaxes and cleavers  (iv) Flake tools and points
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lower: handaxes, cleavers; Middle: flake tools, scrapers, points; Upper: blades, burins; Mesolithic: microliths, hence a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii (निम्न, मध्य, उच्च पुरापाषाण और मध्यपाषाण के उपकरण)

 

• Tools become smaller and more refined as we move from Lower Palaeolithic to Mesolithic.

 

• Microliths are tiny stone tools usually not longer than five centimetres.

 

• This sequence is a favourite for match-the-following questions.

 

• A useful memory aid is to read the match in order: the oldest phase has the heaviest tools, and each later phase has lighter and more specialised ones, until the Mesolithic ends the sequence with tiny microliths.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• In match questions, scrapers and points belong to the Middle Palaeolithic, and scrapers also appear in the Upper phase.

 

• If a column lists microliths, it will almost certainly be paired with the Mesolithic.

 

• Handaxe and cleaver always point to the Lower Palaeolithic in the notes.

 

• Burins are the engraving tool of the Upper Palaeolithic, which helps in elimination.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii (Option 1): This swaps the tools of the Lower and Middle phases by giving flake tools to the Lower and handaxes to the Middle Palaeolithic. This swaps Lower and Middle Palaeolithic tools.

 

• a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii (Option 2): This swaps the Middle and Upper phases by giving blades to the Middle and flake tools to the Upper Palaeolithic. This swaps Middle and Upper Palaeolithic tools.

 

• a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii (Option 3): This ties Lower Palaeolithic with microliths and Mesolithic with handaxes, reversing the order of the oldest and the later tool types. This pairs Mesolithic with handaxes and Lower Palaeolithic with microliths, which is reversed.

question: Bellary, where Palaeolithic remains have been found, is located in which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Karnataka.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Bellary in Karnataka is a noted Palaeolithic site; the other site named in the notes is Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh (बेल्लारी — कर्नाटक; पुरापाषाण स्थल)

 

• Palaeolithic remains are the stone tools of hunter-gatherers.

 

• Bellary lies in the Deccan plateau region of Karnataka.

 

• Bhimbetka is the other well-known Palaeolithic site, famous for rock shelters.

 

• Bellary lies in the Karnataka region of the Deccan, and its remains show that Old Stone Age people lived in peninsular India as well as in central India, so Palaeolithic culture was not confined to the north.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Bhimbetka, in Madhya Pradesh, is the other Palaeolithic site named in the notes, and the pair Bhimbetka-Bellary is a standard exam link.

 

• Karnataka is a southern state; its Palaeolithic remains show that the Old Stone Age extended into peninsular India.

 

• Bellary also appears in questions on Karnataka's geography, as it is an iron-ore mining region of the state.

 

• Do not confuse Palaeolithic Bellary with the Mesolithic Adamgarh in Madhya Pradesh.

 

NOTE

 

• Madhya Pradesh (Option 2): Madhya Pradesh has the Palaeolithic site of Bhimbetka in Raisen district, but Bellary is not located there. Madhya Pradesh has Bhimbetka, but Bellary is not there.

 

• Rajasthan (Option 3): Rajasthan has the Mesolithic site of Bagor and the Chalcolithic sites of Ganeshwar and Ahar, but not Bellary. Rajasthan has Bagor (Mesolithic) and Ganeshwar (Chalcolithic), not Bellary.

 

• Bihar (Option 4): Bihar is known for the Neolithic site of Chirand, not for the Palaeolithic remains of Bellary. Bihar has Chirand (Neolithic), not Bellary. Chirand lies on the Ganga plain and is a Neolithic site with bone tools, which places it in a later age than Bellary.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Palaeolithic Age:

1. People practised agriculture on a small scale.

2. Their stone tools were hand-sized pieces flaked off large pebbles.

3. Their food came from hunting and gathering edible plants and tubers.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2 and 3 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statements 2 and 3 are correct: Palaeolithic people made hand-sized stone tools from large pebbles and lived on hunting and gathering; agriculture was not practised (कथन 2 और 3 सही — पुरापाषाण में कृषि नहीं)

 

• Statement 1 is wrong because nobody farmed in the Palaeolithic Age.

 

• Cultivation began in the Mesolithic (early forms) and became established in the Neolithic.

 

• Palaeolithic remains are found at Bhimbetka (MP) and Bellary (Karnataka).

 

• The verdict on the three statements follows a simple rule: anything about farming, pottery or domestication is a later feature and cannot be a Palaeolithic one, while hunting-gathering and hand-sized pebble tools are the defining Palaeolithic traits.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• A short way to evaluate such statements is to ask whether each item needs settled life; if it does, it is not Palaeolithic.

 

• Palaeolithic stone tools were hand-sized, flaked from large pebbles, and used to hunt animals.

 

• Early cultivation is a Mesolithic beginning, and settled agriculture a Neolithic feature.

 

• The Palaeolithic period is dated before 10000 BC in the notes.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 2 only (Option 1): Statement 2 is correct but statement 1 is false because Palaeolithic people did not farm; this option also wrongly leaves out statement 3. Statement 1 is false, so any option including it is wrong; this also omits statement 3.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): Statement 3 is correct but statement 1 is false because agriculture was absent in the Palaeolithic; this option also leaves out statement 2. Statement 1 is false (no agriculture in Palaeolithic), and statement 3 is true, so this is wrong.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Including statement 1 makes this wrong, since Palaeolithic people lived by hunting and gathering and did not practise agriculture. Statement 1 is false, so 'all three' is wrong.

question: The bow and arrow came into use in which period?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mesolithic.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The bow and arrow came into use in the Mesolithic (Middle Stone Age) period, along with tiny microliths used as arrowheads (धनुष-बाण — मध्यपाषाण काल)

 

• Mesolithic people still lived by hunting and gathering.

 

• The Mesolithic period is dated about 10000 BC to 6000 BC.

 

• The new weapon improved hunting from a distance.

 

• The bow and arrow let hunters strike from a distance, and its tiny stone points are the microliths that give the Mesolithic its identity; it represents a leap in hunting technology over handheld pebble tools.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The bow and arrow is a Mesolithic invention along with microliths, and the notes list both under this period.

 

• Domestication of the dog is another first of the Mesolithic.

 

• Ochre colours in rock paintings are noted for prehistoric India in general.

 

• Mesolithic sites include Adamgarh in Madhya Pradesh and Bagor in Rajasthan.

 

NOTE

 

• Palaeolithic (Option 2): Palaeolithic people used large hand-sized pebble tools and had no bow and arrow; their hunting relied on handheld stone tools. Palaeolithic people used hand-sized pebble tools like handaxes, not the bow and arrow.

 

• Neolithic (Option 3): Neolithic people are known for polished stone tools, farming and pottery; the bow and arrow had appeared earlier in the Mesolithic. Neolithic people are known for polished tools, agriculture and pottery.

 

• Chalcolithic (Option 4): People of the Chalcolithic age worked copper together with stone with stone, and the bow and arrow was already an old invention by then. Chalcolithic people used copper along with stone tools.

question: Which type of weapons were commonly used by Mesolithic people for hunting?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Barbed spears.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mesolithic people used tiny stone microliths fixed into barbed spears and arrows for hunting (काँटेदार भाले — मध्यपाषाण काल, सूक्ष्म पाषाण उपकरण)

 

• Microliths are very small stone tools, usually not bigger than five centimetres.

 

• They were fitted into wood or bone to make composite hunting weapons.

 

• Swords, cannons and catapults belong to much later periods.

 

• A barbed spear carries small stone microliths fixed along or at the tip of a wooden shaft, so a damaged edge can be replaced by a new piece. Such composite weapons are a mark of Mesolithic technology.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Microlith means small stone; the notes describe them as tiny pieces usually no bigger than five centimetres.

 

• Barbed spears and arrows are the typical microlithic weapons listed in the notes.

 

• The Mesolithic is dated about 10000 BC to 6000 BC.

 

• This question pattern has been asked in SSC CGL, so a microlith-weapon link deserves review.

 

NOTE

 

• Swords (Option 1): Swords are made of metal and are weapons of later metal-using and historic societies, so they cannot belong to the Stone Age. Swords are metal weapons of later periods, not the Stone Age.

 

• Cannons (Option 3): Cannons depend on gunpowder and came into Indian warfare only in the medieval period, many thousands of years after the Mesolithic. Cannons use gunpowder and appeared in medieval times.

 

• Catapults (Option 4): Catapults are siege engines of later historic warfare, not the simple weapons of Mesolithic hunters. Catapults are siege engines of later historical periods. The catapult, in the sense of a siege machine, was used in later wars to hurl stones at fort walls, long after the Stone Age.

question: Which was the first animal domesticated by humans, becoming their first pet?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dog.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The dog was the first animal kept as a pet by humans, a development of the Mesolithic period (कुत्ता — पहला पालतू पशु, मध्यपाषाण काल)

 

• Mesolithic people began staying in one place for longer stretches, leading to domestication and early cultivation.

 

• Dogs helped in hunting and guarding settlements.

 

• Adamgarh (MP) gives the earliest evidence of animal domestication in India.

 

• Keeping animals demands a settled life, because herds have to be fed and protected. The dog was the first animal to be tamed, probably because it helped in hunting, and later herd animals followed during the farming phases.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The dog's domestication is a typical Mesolithic first, while farm animals follow in the Neolithic.

 

• Domestication of animals is one of the four main features of the Neolithic Age.

 

• Animal husbandry evidence also comes from Bagor in Rajasthan.

 

• First pet and first metal are two similar-looking firsts: dog for animals and copper for metals.

 

NOTE

 

• Cow (Option 1): Cattle were domesticated later with the spread of farming, and the cow was not the first animal to become a human companion. Cattle were domesticated later, mainly with Neolithic farming.

 

• Horse (Option 2): The horse was domesticated much later than the dog and is not regarded as the first tamed animal. Horse domestication is much later and is not linked with the Mesolithic pet stage.

 

• Sheep (Option 3): Sheep were domesticated by early farming and herding communities after the dog, so they were not the first. Sheep were domesticated with Neolithic farming communities, after the dog.

question: Which Mesolithic site in Madhya Pradesh gives the earliest evidence of animal domestication?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Adamgarh.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Adamgarh (Madhya Pradesh) gives the earliest evidence of animal domestication, a major Mesolithic site (आदमगढ़ — पशुपालन के प्राचीनतम साक्ष्य)

 

• Bagor in Rajasthan also gave evidence of animal husbandry.

 

• Bhimbetka in MP is another site of the Mesolithic period with rock shelters.

 

• These sites show a gradual shift from pure hunting to herding.

 

• Adamgarh and Bagor are often asked together, so remember the contrast: Adamgarh in Madhya Pradesh is cited for the earliest evidence of domestication of animals, Bagor in Rajasthan for animal husbandry.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Adamgarh is a hill site in the Hoshangabad area of Madhya Pradesh, and it appears in lists of Mesolithic rock shelters.

 

• Bagor in Rajasthan, on the river Kothari, is another important Mesolithic site.

 

• Bhimbetka also has Mesolithic remains, so it can be asked together with Adamgarh.

 

• Sites like Navdatoli and Burzahom are later, so they act as distractors.

 

NOTE

 

• Bagor (Option 1): Bagor is in Rajasthan, not Madhya Pradesh, although it also gave evidence of animal husbandry; the question specifically asks about the earliest evidence in Madhya Pradesh. Bagor is in Rajasthan, not Madhya Pradesh, though it also has evidence of animal husbandry.

 

• Burzahom (Option 2): Burzahom is a Neolithic site in the Kashmir valley, known for pit dwellings, and is not a Mesolithic site of Madhya Pradesh. Burzahom is a Neolithic site in the Kashmir valley.

 

• Navdatoli (Option 4): Navdatoli is a Chalcolithic site on the Narmada in Madhya Pradesh, famed for painted pottery, and belongs to a later age than the Mesolithic. Navdatoli is a Chalcolithic site on the Narmada known for painted pottery.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Mesolithic Age:

1. People continued to live by hunting and gathering.

2. Microliths were used.

3. People settled in one place for longer, leading to animal domestication and early cultivation.

Which of the above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• All statements are correct for the Mesolithic (10000-6000 BC): hunting-gathering continued, microliths appeared, and longer stays at one place led to domestication, horticulture and early cultivation (मध्यपाषाण — सूक्ष्म पाषाण, पशुपालन)

 

• The bow and arrow also came into use in this period.

 

• The dog became the first pet animal.

 

• Settled life became permanent only with Neolithic farming.

 

• Notice that hunting-gathering still continues in the Mesolithic. The change is one of degree: more time spent in one place, small tools, and the first steps towards herding and growing plants.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Horticulture means growing fruit and vegetable plants on a small scale, which the notes link with the Mesolithic.

 

• Microliths are the characteristic tools of this phase, and the bow and arrow improved hunting.

 

• The dog helped hunters and was the first tamed animal.

 

• In the Neolithic, farming became the main source of food and villages grew.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 2 only (Option 1): Though statements 1 and 2 are accurate, dropping statement 3 is an error: longer stays at one place let Mesolithic people keep animals and start horticulture, with Adamgarh and Bagor as evidence.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 2): While statements 2 and 3 are accurate, dropping statement 1 is an error: the Mesolithic economy was still hunting and gathering, and the dog, bow and arrow only improved it rather than replacing it.

 

• 3 only (Option 3): Only statement 3 is not enough, because statements 1 and 2 about hunting-gathering and microliths are also correct. This omits statements 1 and 2, which are also correct.

question: Which colours of ochre were commonly used in the prehistoric rock paintings found in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Black, white and red.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Black, white and red ochre were commonly used in prehistoric rock paintings found in India, e.g. at Bhimbetka (काला, सफेद और लाल गेरू — शैलचित्र)

 

• Ochre is a natural earth pigment, rich in iron oxide, which gives red or yellowish-brown shades.

 

• The paintings show animals and birds and were made using stones and bones.

 

• Bhimbetka in the Vindhyanchal range is the best known site of rock paintings.

 

• Ochre is a natural earth pigment, so artists needed no metal or complex technology to make colours. Paintings at Bhimbetka were made with such pigments on rock-shelter walls with simple tools.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rock shelters often served as homes as well as galleries for the paintings.

 

• Paintings were made with stones and bones, according to the notes.

 

• Black, white and red are the colours to remember for questions on pigments.

 

• Red ochre is the commonest of the three in prehistoric Indian rock art.

 

NOTE

 

• Blue, green and yellow (Option 1): Blue, green and yellow are not the colours listed in the notes; prehistoric Indian rock art mainly used black, white and red ochre. Blue, green and yellow are not the standard colours of prehistoric Indian rock paintings.

 

• Purple, pink and orange (Option 3): Purple, pink and orange were not the commonly used pigments of prehistoric rock paintings in India. Purple, pink and orange were not the commonly used pigments.

 

• Gold, silver and bronze (Option 4): Gold, silver and bronze are metals, not pigments, and metals were unknown to Stone Age painters. Gold, silver and bronze are metals, not pigments used in prehistoric painting.

question: The Mesolithic Age in India is dated approximately to:
solution_text:
The correct answer is 10000 BC - 6000 BC.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Mesolithic Age (Middle Stone Age) is dated 10000 BC to 6000 BC, between the Palaeolithic and the Neolithic (मध्यपाषाण काल — 10000-6000 ई.पू.)

 

• Meso means middle and lithic means stone.

 

• Its hallmark is the microlith, a very small stone tool usually below five centimetres.

 

• Life began to change as people stayed longer in one place.

 

• The Mesolithic is a bridge between the long Palaeolithic and the farming Neolithic on any timeline. Its date range, 10000 BC to 6000 BC, is worth memorising.

 

• The span of 10000 BC to 6000 BC makes the Mesolithic a transitional phase between the long hunting-gathering Palaeolithic and the farming Neolithic.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Palaeolithic ends at about 10000 BC, where the Mesolithic begins.

 

• The Neolithic follows from about 6000 BC in the notes' scheme.

 

• Microliths, bow and arrow, dog domestication and early cultivation are the Mesolithic markers.

 

• A clear timeline helps with questions that ask which period matches a date range.

 

• The Mesolithic is often confused with the Neolithic because both mention settling down, but only the Neolithic has full agriculture, so check the date range and the main economy before choosing an option.

 

NOTE

 

• Before 10000 BC (Option 1): Before 10000 BC is the span of the Palaeolithic Age, the Old Stone Age of hunter-gatherers with large pebble tools. Before 10000 BC is the Palaeolithic Age.

 

• 6000 BC - 1000 BC (Option 2): 6000 BC onwards in the notes' scheme is the Neolithic Age, which brings agriculture, pottery and polished tools. 6000 BC onwards is the Neolithic Age in the notes' scheme.

 

• 3000 BC - 1000 BC (Option 3): 3000 BC to 1000 BC is the notes' span for Protohistory, a division based on writing rather than on stone-tool phases. 3000-1000 BC is the span of Protohistory, not the Mesolithic.

question: Which of the following is NOT a Mesolithic site?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Burzahom.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Burzahom in the Kashmir valley is a Neolithic site; Adamgarh, Bagor and Bhimbetka are Mesolithic sites (बुर्जहोम — नवपाषाण स्थल)

 

• Adamgarh (MP) gives the earliest evidence of animal domestication.

 

• Bagor (Rajasthan) shows evidence of animal husbandry.

 

• Bhimbetka (MP) has famous rock shelters and paintings.

 

• Questions of this kind exploit the common confusion between sites and ages. Always attach each site to its age: Adamgarh, Bagor and Bhimbetka to the Mesolithic, and Burzahom to the Neolithic.

 

• The other three sites in the options are Mesolithic centres in Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, which is why the odd-one-out is the site from the Kashmir valley.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Burzahom in Kashmir is famous for its early village life and pit dwellings.

 

• Bhimbetka's Mesolithic layers show hunting and gathering with small stone tools.

 

• Adamgarh and Bagor are both associated with domestication.

 

• The odd-one-out pattern appears often: three sites of one age and one from another.

 

• Burzahom's Neolithic people lived in pits dug into the ground, which is a famous feature of the site; this pit-dwelling detail separates Burzahom from the rock-shelter sites of the Mesolithic.

 

NOTE

 

• Adamgarh (Option 1): Adamgarh in Madhya Pradesh is a Mesolithic site giving the earliest evidence of animal domestication, so it is not the exception. Adamgarh is a Mesolithic site in Madhya Pradesh.

 

• Bagor (Option 2): Bagor in Rajasthan is a Mesolithic site where domestication and animal husbandry were found, so it is not the exception. Bagor is a Mesolithic site in Rajasthan.

 

• Bhimbetka (Option 4): Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh has Mesolithic rock shelters and paintings (besides Palaeolithic remains), so it is not the exception. Bhimbetka is a Mesolithic site (also with Palaeolithic remains) in Madhya Pradesh.

question:
Assertion (A): Animal domestication and early cultivation began during the Mesolithic Age.

Reason (R): Mesolithic people started staying in one place for longer stretches of time.

Select the correct option:
option_1: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true, but R is false
option_4: A is false, but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both are true and R explains A: as people began staying longer in one place, animal domestication, horticulture and early forms of cultivation began in the Mesolithic (मध्यपाषाण — स्थायी निवास से पशुपालन)

 

• Staying put gave time to tend plants and keep animals.

 

• The dog was the first animal kept as a pet.

 

• Full-fledged agriculture and permanent villages are Neolithic features.

 

• Staying at one place is the hinge of the argument: it created a link between humans and the plants and animals around them, and this link slowly grew into the farming economy that matured in the Neolithic.

 

• The two statements are linked by the idea of settled life, which is the single key to all questions on the transition from hunting to farming.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Mesolithic shift towards staying longer in one place prepared the ground for the Neolithic revolution.

 

• Horticulture and early forms of cultivation are linked with this stage.

 

• Dog domestication is the commonly asked Mesolithic first.

 

• A true explanation question depends on spotting the causal link, which is present here.

 

• Cause-and-effect questions in this chapter follow one chain: longer stay at a place, then care of plants and animals, then domestication and cultivation, and finally full agriculture in the Neolithic.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 2): R is not just a related fact; staying longer in one place gave people the time to tend plants and keep animals, so it directly explains A. R is the real cause behind A, so it is the correct explanation.

 

• A is true, but R is false (Option 3): R is also true, since Mesolithic people began staying in one place for longer stretches, so it cannot be called false. R is true, so the 'A is true, but R is false' option fails.

 

• A is false, but R is true (Option 4): A is true because domestication and early cultivation did begin in the Mesolithic, so the assertion cannot be called false. A is true as the notes state domestication and early cultivation began, so 'A is false' fails.

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four main features of the Neolithic Age?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Use of iron tools.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The four main features of the Neolithic Age are agriculture, animal domestication, polished stone tools and pottery; iron tools are not a Neolithic feature (नवपाषाण — लौह उपकरण नहीं)

 

• Neolithic people used polished stone tools, not metal ones.

 

• Iron came into use in much later periods.

 

• Copper was the first metal humans discovered, in the Chalcolithic phase.

 

• The only item that does not fit the Neolithic list is metal: the Neolithic is still a stone age, with tools polished smooth, while metal use begins with copper in the Chalcolithic phase.

 

• The other three listed items are the real features of the Neolithic, so only the metal-tool statement fails the test in a NOT-type question.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Metals begin with copper in the Chalcolithic, and iron comes still later.

 

• Polished stone tools are a distinct Neolithic feature.

 

• Pottery manufacture helps with cooking and storing grain.

 

• Domestication of animals and agriculture are the economic features of the Neolithic.

 

• Neolithic features are always listed as four items: agriculture, domestication of animals, polished stone tools and pottery; any option naming iron or copper tools belongs to a later metal age.

 

NOTE

 

• Practice of agriculture (Option 1): Agriculture is the first listed feature of the Neolithic Age and is the basis of permanent settlements, so it is not the exception. Agriculture is a key Neolithic feature.

 

• Domestication of animals (Option 3): Domestication of animals is a Neolithic feature along with farming, so it is not the exception. Domestication of animals is a Neolithic feature. Early herding, with the dog first and farm animals later, is why this item is a genuine part of the Neolithic list.

 

• Manufacture of pottery (Option 4): Pottery manufacture is a Neolithic feature, needed for storing grain and cooking, so it is not the exception. Pottery manufacture is a Neolithic feature. Clay pots, often hand-made at first, allowed grain to be stored and cooked, which is why pottery is one of the four listed features.
